# The *diagnosis*.

::: callout-important
## In Brief

This chapter is a diagnostic. You'll name what's actually broken in your company's AI approach — and it's not the tools, the training, or the team. It's the operating model. By the end you'll have a scored AI Readiness Scorecard across five dimensions, a clear picture of where to start, and the honest answer to a question most leadership teams avoid: are we actually ready to operate differently?
:::

We learned most of it from one question.

We were on a discovery call with a long-time client, a mid-size manufacturing company, about fifty people, eight-figure revenue. The CEO and two of his direct reports were on the screen. We asked how they were using AI. The CEO said ChatGPT. One director said Claude. The other said Poe, an aggregator that lets you sample models without committing to one.

Three people. One company. Three different tools. No shared accounts or projects, no shared workflow. Each of them had gone out and found something on their own, the same way someone downloads a new app to try it out. And each of them was using it the same way: individually, occasionally, for whatever felt useful in the moment.

We asked what they were hoping AI would do for the business. The answer was honest: they had a gut sense that AI could be doing more for the company, but they didn't know what was even possible. They booked the call precisely because they didn't know what they wanted, only that they were leaving something on the table.

This is a design problem, not a technology problem. It's the most common version of the AI problem we see: three people, three tools, no coordination, no structural change. No one designed the work before the tool arrived.

The design we mean is the *operating model*: how work actually moves through your company. Who decides what gets done, who hands what to whom, what each function is accountable for. The org chart names the boxes. The operating model is how work moves between them.

We've watched this same pattern for two decades, long before AI entered the conversation. A mid-market company would complete an acquisition and absorb the new entity without redesigning how work actually moved. The acquired operation got bolted onto the existing structure, with the same managers handling expanded volume. The accountability map was never rebuilt to match the expanded scope. AI is just the latest technology to expose a problem that's been visible the whole time.

This pattern is common. It might describe your company.

> You know AI matters. You just don't know what it can actually do inside your company — or where to start.

That sentence isn't a secret. CEOs say it all the time: to their boards, their coaches, their peers at dinner. They know AI matters, they've started looking, and they still can't find the entry point that makes sense for the business they run. This book exists to provide that clarity. We've watched this happen inside our own companies and inside the companies we work with: agents doing real work, smaller teams shipping more, the cost curve of knowledge work bending in ways that no longer feel theoretical. But the gap between that reality and what you're supposed to *do* on a Tuesday morning, inside the company you run, is where most operators get stuck.

It's not for lack of effort. You bought subscriptions. Maybe you ran a pilot or two, brought in a consultant, sat through a vendor demo. What you've got to show for it is a tool your team barely uses and a handful of use cases that never scaled. Nobody showed you how to design the work.

We were on a call with a company that runs on EOS (the Entrepreneurial Operating System): Accountability Chart, scorecards, L10 meetings, the works. A disciplined company. And even here, they couldn't frame the AI problem, let alone implement a solution. They had AI subscriptions across the team. One marketing lead was building an agent in Microsoft Copilot on her own time, after hours. An agent is a configured workflow that takes actions and runs steps on its own, without a human typing every prompt (more on this in Chapter 2). Everyone else was using AI as a sounding board. No workflow had changed. No output was different. When we asked who in the organization could drive their AI initiative, the owner paused and said four words: "I don't have that person." AI requires a different kind of design than anything their operating model was built to handle.

One person working harder inside a system that was never designed for AI is not adoption.

The instinct is to blame adoption, or to blame the tool itself. *AI can't do X. It's not ready for our industry.* That diagnosis is comfortable because it avoids fixing the operating model. Acting on it produces exactly one outcome: another training session that also doesn't work.

The real problem is upstream of adoption, and it has two parts. The first: the company has no designed structure for a non-human worker to operate inside. Nobody built that before the AI subscriptions started. The second is just as common and rarely named. Operators don't yet have a clear picture of what AI can actually do inside a business like theirs. They've seen the demos. They've read the headlines. They haven't seen what a designed agent workflow looks like in their own operation, with their own data, hitting their own numbers. So the asks stay small, and the design conversation never starts.

To harness AI, traditionally non-technical and bricks-and-mortar businesses have to learn structures that software companies have used for years: treating workflows as systems, knowledge as an indexed asset, and handoffs as designed interfaces. That means new terms, new processes, and a different understanding of how knowledge flows through an organization in digital form. Part of the evolution is education. This book is partly that education, combining the operating patterns you already run with the operating patterns of fast-growing tech-enabled companies.

## The Headcount *Paradox*.

Here is the math you're living right now.

The company is growing. The pipeline is healthy. So your leadership team is asking to hire. Another account manager. Another ops person. Another engineer. The assumption underneath is that growth means adding people. Automation is familiar in manufacturing, where machines replaced repetitive physical work. It's less familiar in the information economy, where the work requires judgment. And it's almost entirely unfamiliar in an intelligence economy, where decisions themselves can be assisted or handled by a non-human worker. When operators think about software here, they think about moving data between systems, maybe Zapier, maybe an integration. They aren't yet thinking about AI for work that requires decisions. But now they can.

You've bought some AI: a ChatGPT subscription, maybe an automation tool, maybe a consultant for a few hours. You didn't bet the farm. Most operators haven't. The spend has been small. You're willing to invest more. The budget is there. The intent is there. But you don't know where to aim, what to buy, what to build, or what return to expect.

Revenue and headcount run on a slope: every meaningful jump in revenue pulls a roughly proportional jump in headcount along with it. That slope was steep in 2022, and for most mid-market operators the AI line item on the P&L, small as it is, hasn't done anything to bend it. A handful of enterprises that have taken this work seriously are already seeing the slope start to flatten in specific functions. The pattern hasn't reached the middle market yet, which is who this book is for.

The slope has a name. Divide revenue by headcount and you get revenue per employee, the metric that sits under the paradox. In most companies it stays roughly flat as they grow: each new dollar of revenue arrives with about the same amount of human labor attached to it. Every company can calculate this number today. What this book is about is moving it.

Meanwhile your COO (Integrator if you run EOS) is on the calendar asking to approve the next two roles. The numbers in the request aren't unreasonable: the work is real, the team is stretched, the demand is there. You sign off, because the alternative is throttling growth, and throttling growth isn't a strategy. But you sign off knowing the AI investment was supposed to bend that slope by now, and you can't point to the reason it didn't.

The Headcount Paradox: each new dollar of revenue still demands roughly the same headcount it did before, even after you invested in AI to change that math. The investment is on the books, and it hasn't changed the structure.

### How the math finally moves.

Here's how it resolved at Jesse's company. SuperWebPros, his software development firm, went from thirteen people to eight. We mapped every function, identified what required human judgment and what didn't, built agent teams for rule-based work, and kept humans on work that required taste, relationships, and strategic decisions. Billings went up. Profitability went up.

Five people left the company. They weren't laid off in a single round, and we worked to place several of them well. But those five seats are gone, because the work they existed to do now runs on systems we designed. At Jesse's company the slope inverted. The more common version is less extreme and just as valuable: the team grows slower than the top line, so the marginal headcount per next dollar of revenue drops. That's the Headcount Math moving the way it's supposed to.

That same math can work at very different scales. When a global food safety company completed a Fortune 500 division acquisition, Julie was the CHRO overseeing the integration across 44 countries. The instinct in every integration conversation was to add HR business partners by region. The alternative was to redesign the operating model first — making a deliberate decision about which HR functions required local human judgment and which could run on a standardized system. The resulting global HR function served 44 countries with a smaller proportional team than the pre-acquisition domestic function had. Not because headcount was cut. Because the work was designed before it was staffed.

::: callout-tip
## Pro Tip
The Headcount Paradox doesn't break by adding AI to the existing org chart. It breaks by redesigning the org chart so AI has a seat on it. That's what changes the slope.
:::

{{< excalidraw ch01-headcount-before-after "The Headcount Paradox: the slope before redesign vs. the slope after — revenue climbs faster than headcount when work is designed before it's staffed." >}}

When AI investments don't pay off, the first instinct is to blame the tools — to assume the technology was oversold or that next quarter's version will finally do the thing. But the tools are more capable than most operators realize. The problem is that there's no defined relationship between the AI system and the work it's supposed to do. There's no designed workflow, no clear accountability, and no governance. The tool sits in the background and helps individuals occasionally, but it doesn't change the structure of the work. Structural change is what moves the math.

## It looks like a *technology* problem. It's actually an *operating* problem.

Your AI investments aren't producing returns because of an operating-model problem. Specifically, a Co-Intelligent Co-Operation problem.

The diagnosis is a *Co-Intelligent Co-Operation problem*. *Co-Intelligent* is the actual workforce: humans and AI as one system, defined in Chapter 2. *Co-Operation* is the structural work of getting that workforce to operate together. The *problem* is the gap between the two.

Culture matters: a team that resists change will stall any initiative. Training matters: people need to know what the tools can do. Tool selection matters: the wrong platform creates its own drag. These are all real, but the deeper problem is the operating model. The company was designed, deliberately or by drift, to be run by humans alone. You then introduced a second kind of worker, synthetic, capable, available, and dropped it next to the structure without changing the structure. The new worker has no seat, no accountability, and no defined handoff. So it produces nothing the organization can compound on. Culture, training, and tools are necessary. The missing piece is structural redesign.

This failure has the same shape across thirty years of operating-model changes, long before AI. ERP rollouts are the clearest example: companies spent eight-figure sums to install new systems, then left the old reporting structures and decision rights exactly as they were. The system sat live while people worked around it. The pattern isn't that the technology failed. The capability arrived and the structure never changed to receive it. The new thing sat next to the old structure and produced nothing structural. AI is the latest technology to run into the same wall — the only difference is the speed and cost of the collision.

Most people still think of AI as a chatbot, a thing you type questions into and read answers from. In most companies, that's exactly the relationship: one human, one chat window, one task at a time. The human is micromanaging the AI the same way they'd micromanage a junior employee, hovering over every output, typing every instruction. It might be slightly more productive, but it's not compounding anything because the human is still the bottleneck.

The real capability is in agents — the kind defined earlier: workflows that take actions and run steps on their own, where the design says which moves require a human review and which don't. An agent can research, draft, route, check, escalate, and deliver, all inside a designed system. And agents can run in parallel. While you're reviewing one deliverable, three other workstreams are moving. A chatbot answers questions. An agent does work. If your mental model of AI is still the chatbot, you're underestimating what's possible.

EOS, Scaling Up, and other disciplined systems are built on this shape: an Accountability Chart, scorecards, and the L10 (EOS's weekly leadership meeting) or its equivalent. Work added without a named owner dies in the gap. AI is no different. It's a new kind of worker added to the system without anyone naming who owns it, what it's accountable for, or where the handoffs live. So it dies in the gap, the same way any unowned function does.

Walk into any function in your company today and ask the same three questions you'd ask of a human team: what is this function accountable for, what is its scorecard, who reviews the output and on what cadence. You'd get clean answers for the humans and blank stares for the AI. The AI in your company has no seat on the chart, no number it's hitting, and no review rhythm. You wouldn't run a function staffed by people that way. You're running the AI that way because you haven't yet treated it as staff.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Walk into your next L10 or leadership meeting with this question: "If AI were an employee, what would its scorecard say?" Write down whatever the room produces. If the room can't answer — if there's no scorecard, no number, no owner — that's your answer. There is no scorecard. And that's exactly the problem.
:::

> The instinct to solve a people problem with another person is exactly the instinct this book exists to interrupt.

None of this is mysterious. All of it is operating work, not technology work. The frame is the operating model itself.

## The wrong *question*.

Every organization falls into the same trap at the start of its AI effort.

The first question most teams ask is task-oriented: *which of our existing tasks could AI help with?* It gets you some of the way there. You'll find prompt tips, a few useful shortcuts, some real time saved. Using AI to write a social media post is a fine task. But task-orientation is insufficient. It adds AI on top of the existing workflow, and that workflow was designed for humans. The gains stay small and scattered, and nothing changes structurally.

Companies that get this right end up with the Headcount Math working in their favor. Revenue and profitability climb while the team's growth rate decouples from the top line. The discipline behind that result is straightforward: start with the outcome the organization is accountable for, then design the work backward from that outcome. A single question drives the whole exercise: who owns what step, and does that step require judgment or follow a rule? The answer tells you where AI belongs and where it doesn't. Skipping the outcome and design steps and going straight to tools is what produces the scattered use cases and the stalled pilots. This discipline predates AI. The AI era made the cost of skipping it visible.

The question that unlocks real value is goal-oriented: *what outcomes are we accountable for, and how should the human + AI workforce be designed to deliver them?* That question doesn't start with the tools. It starts with outcomes, and then with accountability for those outcomes. It produces a deliberate design: who owns what, what the human reviews, what the agent team executes, where the handoff lives, how the result gets measured. Writing a social post is a task. Building a sustainable content production workflow that reinforces itself regardless of who's sitting in the seat is a bigger problem with a much bigger payoff.

::: callout-tip
## Pro Tip

If your AI initiative starts with "what tasks can AI do?" you'll get a list of tasks. If it starts with "what outcomes do we need, and who — human or AI — should own each one?" you'll get an operating model.
:::

{{< excalidraw ch01-wrong-vs-right-question "The Wrong Question vs. The Right Question" >}}

## Where you actually *stand*.

The AI Readiness Scorecard tells you where you stand.

The AI Readiness Scorecard covers five dimensions of operational readiness. For each one, you'll score yourself Red, Yellow, or Green.

Do this with whoever would be in the room if you were deciding whether to invest in AI. Not just you, the team.

A note before you start: you may not be able to answer all five of these cleanly. The scorecard shows you where you're starting. A Red score is the starting point most companies are at, and the rest of this book is built to move you forward from there.

We'll define every term as we go. For now, a "constraint" means the one operational pain point your company keeps hitting: the thing your team keeps circling in meetings, the process that breaks when one person is out, the workflow where you feel the drag every week. Sometimes that pain is the biggest dollar cost on the P&L. Often it isn't. It might be the risk that keeps you up at night, the bottleneck that caps growth in a key account, the dependency on one person that you can't afford to lose. The cost matters and we'll get to the math in Dimension 5. The pain is what tells you where to look first.

The five dimensions sit inside two preconditions. Information Readiness and Workflow Visibility are the *technical preconditions* that determine whether an AI agent can actually do the work: whether the knowledge exists in a form the system can reach, and whether the workflow is mapped clearly enough to be handed off. Constraint Clarity, Decision Rights, and Measurement Discipline are the *operating-model preconditions* that determine whether your organization will hold the change once it's deployed: whether your team agrees on what to solve, who decides what AI touches, and whether you can measure the result. A company can score Green on the technical side and Red on the operating side. It can have leadership clarity and no documented workflow. Both halves have to be Green before a Sprint will hold.

### Dimension 1: Constraint Clarity

*Can your leadership team name the ONE operational constraint AI should solve?*

| Score | What it looks like |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Red** | No clear constraint. The team talks about AI in general terms ("we should use AI") but can't name a specific operational problem it would solve. |
| **Yellow** | Multiple candidates, no priority. The issues list has several items that "could benefit from AI," but the team hasn't ranked them or committed to one. |
| **Green** | One validated constraint with a cost. The team can name the constraint in one sentence and attach a dollar figure to it. |

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Don't ask your leadership team what AI should solve. They don't know yet, and neither did you before you picked up this book. Ask them a question they *can* answer: "What is the one operational problem we keep circling and never close, the one that hurts the most, whether it shows up in dollars, hours, risk, or a person we can't afford to lose?" Poll each person individually, write down the answers verbatim, and compare. If five people give five different answers, you've found something more useful than a constraint. You've found the leadership-team disagreement that any AI work would have run into anyway. Chapter 4 turns that raw answer into a usable constraint statement.
:::

The poll results tell you more than any scorecard row. Agreement on the operational pain means you've got a starting point. Disagreement means the constraint isn't the workflow yet; it's the leadership team's agreement on what matters most.

::: callout-tip
## Pro Tip

If your leadership team can't agree on the constraint, that disagreement IS the diagnosis. No AI tool fixes misaligned priorities.
:::

### Dimension 2: Information Readiness

*Is the knowledge your team runs on documented and accessible, or trapped in people's heads?*

| Score | What it looks like |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Red** | Mostly tribal. The way things get done lives in the heads of a few key people. When they're out, things slow down or break. |
| **Yellow** | Partially documented. Some processes are written down, but the critical knowledge (pricing logic, client history, escalation paths) still depends on specific individuals. |
| **Green** | Documented and indexed. Processes, decisions, and institutional knowledge are written down, stored in systems the team can access, and maintained regularly. |

If your best operations person quit tomorrow, how long before the replacement could run the workflow without calling them? If the answer is "months," you're Red regardless of what's in your wiki.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Pick your most critical workflow. Ask the person who owns it: "If you had to hand this off to someone new on Monday, what would you give them?" Whatever they describe is the actual state of your documentation — not whatever lives in SharePoint.
:::

### Dimension 3: Workflow Visibility

*Can you draw the workflow where the constraint lives, including who does what and where handoffs break?*

| Score | What it looks like |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Red** | Nobody can draw it. The workflow exists as a series of habits and reactions. If you asked three people to map it, you'd get three different maps. |
| **Yellow** | Someone knows it but it's not documented. One or two people could walk you through the workflow, but it lives in their heads and has never been drawn, validated, or shared. |
| **Green** | Documented with ownership. The workflow is mapped, each step has an owner, handoffs are identified, and the team agrees on where it breaks. |

The gap between Yellow and Green here is agreement. A workflow described by one person isn't enough. The team has to validate it, and that's what AI needs to run on.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Whiteboard your most constrained workflow in fifteen minutes. Put every handoff on the board. Circle the ones where work stalls, errors appear, or people say "I'll just handle it myself." Those circles are where the real problem lives.
:::

### Dimension 4: Decision Rights

*Does your team know who decides what AI handles vs. what stays with humans?*

| Score | What it looks like |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Red** | No conversation has happened. The team hasn't discussed which tasks AI could take over, which require human judgment, and who makes that call. |
| **Yellow** | Vague ideas. People have opinions about what AI "should" do, but there are no explicit assignments, no written boundaries, and no agreement on who decides. |
| **Green** | Explicit assignments per role. The team has defined which decisions and tasks are AI-eligible, which stay human, and who has authority to change the boundary. |

Decision rights come down to organizational trust, not AI capability. The question is whether you trust the output enough to act on it without a human checking. That's a leadership decision. And not every workflow should aim for full automation. Some workflows should keep a human in the loop. Make that a deliberate choice based on the goal, not a default because nobody designed the alternative.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

List the five most frequent decisions in your constrained workflow. For each one, write down who currently makes the decision and whether it requires judgment or just follows a rule. The rule-based ones are AI-eligible. The judgment ones need a human-in-the-loop design.
:::

### Dimension 5: Measurement Discipline

*Can you put a dollar number on what the constraint costs per quarter?*

| Score | What it looks like |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Red** | Can't quantify. The team knows something is expensive or slow, but can't produce a number. |
| **Yellow** | Rough estimate. Someone can say "it probably costs us around \$X" but the number isn't validated, isn't tracked, and wouldn't survive scrutiny. |
| **Green** | Validated number with data. The cost is calculated from real data (hours tracked, margin analyzed, revenue measured) and the team can show the math. |

If you can't measure what the constraint costs today, you can't measure whether AI made it better tomorrow. Cost here is broader than dollars. It can be hours lost, deals walked, errors caught late, customers who churned quietly, the risk you carry in one person's head. Dollar cost is the cleanest version, and where you can get to it, use it. Where you can't, pick the most honest unit you can defend and measure it the same way every quarter. Without that, you have an AI experiment, not an AI initiative. An initiative has a target.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

Do the math right now. Hours per week spent on the constraint, multiplied by loaded cost per hour, multiplied by thirteen weeks. That's your quarterly cost floor. If you can't fill in the numbers, write down what data you'd need and where you'd get it. That gap is your first task.
:::

### Read your pattern.

Fill in your scorecard:

| Dimension | Score |
|-----------|-------|
| Constraint Clarity | [ R / Y / G ] |
| Information Readiness | [ R / Y / G ] |
| Workflow Visibility | [ R / Y / G ] |
| Decision Rights | [ R / Y / G ] |
| Measurement Discipline | [ R / Y / G ] |

**All Red:** You aren't ready for an AI initiative yet. The Compound Sprint framework exists to move you from Red to Green, dimension by dimension.

**Mixed Red/Yellow:** Start with whichever dimension scored Yellow. Yellow means you've got something to build on: a partial answer, an existing document, a person who already knows the workflow but hasn't written it down. Red means you're building from scratch. That's why your Yellow is your best starting point: the foundation already exists, so turning Yellow to Green is clarification work.

**Mostly Yellow:** The work is clarification and commitment. The Sprint framework will move fast for you.

**Any Green:** Protect it. A Green score means someone did the work to document, quantify, or decide. Build from that foundation — don't let a new initiative overwrite the discipline that produced it.

**All Green:** You don't need the rest of this chapter. Skip to Chapter 4 and run the Sprint.

### What it looks like in practice.

To make the Sequence tangible, we built a fictional company from the real patterns we've seen across dozens of engagements. Meridian Manufacturing will follow you through every chapter of this book, so you can see each stage applied to one continuous example. The full case study is in the appendix if you want to read it straight through.

### Meridian Manufacturing.

Meet Meridian Manufacturing. Seven-point-two million in revenue, twenty-seven employees, custom metal fabrication for industrial clients. Mark Ellison is the CEO. He built the business from a two-person garage shop eighteen years ago and still holds the key customer relationships. Elena Ruiz is his VP of Operations and Integrator. She runs the floor, manages scheduling, and is the only person in the company who can produce a complete quote. The rest of the leadership team: Ty Banfield in sales, Dave Kowalski as senior design engineer (thirty-one years in fabrication), and Carlos Medina running the shop floor.

Meridian runs EOS. Accountability chart, scorecards, L10s, the works. They've grown profitably for years. The constraint: their quotes take three to five days to turn around. Industry standard is twenty-four to forty-eight hours. The full cost of that constraint runs to roughly \$558,000 a year, combining walked bids that cite turnaround time, misallocated senior time, and floor underutilization. The actual number is higher because most clients who go elsewhere don't explain. The bottleneck is Elena. Pricing exceptions live on her desktop. Material lead-times live in her head. She's the only one who can close a quote, and she's getting buried.

Six months ago, Mark bought a ChatGPT subscription. He uses it for emails. He suspects AI could help with the quoting problem but has no idea how to start. That's where we meet them.

| Dimension | Score | What We Found |
|-----------|-------|---------------|
| **Constraint Clarity** | Yellow | The L10 kept circling quoting speed, but the CEO and VP of Ops hadn't agreed it was THE constraint. The issues list had eight items. Quoting was on it — but so were six other things. |
| **Information Readiness** | Red | The VP of Ops WAS the documentation. Pricing exceptions lived in a spreadsheet on her desktop. Material lead-time knowledge was in her head. She was the only person who could produce a complete quote. |
| **Workflow Visibility** | Yellow | The sales lead could draw the front half of quoting. The design engineer could draw the estimation piece. The VP of Ops could draw the whole thing. The three drawings would conflict on at least four steps. |
| **Decision Rights** | Red | The AI conversation hadn't happened. The CEO bought a ChatGPT subscription six months ago. He used it for emails. Nobody had discussed what AI should or shouldn't touch in the quoting workflow. |
| **Measurement Discipline** | Yellow | The sales lead had win/loss data showing lost bids from slow quotes. The VP of Ops had gut estimates on time per quote. Neither number had been validated or tracked as a metric. |

Two Reds, three Yellows. The Yellows told Meridian where to start. Constraint Clarity was Yellow because the quoting bottleneck was already showing up in every L10, but the team hadn't committed to it as the single constraint. Workflow Visibility was Yellow because three people could each draw part of the quoting workflow, but they hadn't agreed on one map. Measurement Discipline was Yellow because the sales lead already had win/loss data that still needed to be validated and turned into a real number.

The Reds were the deeper problems. Information Readiness was Red because one person was the system — pricing exceptions on a desktop spreadsheet, lead-time knowledge in her head, customer-specific terms that no one else could access. AI can't operate inside a system that only exists in someone's head. Decision Rights was Red because the conversation hadn't started. Until a leadership team decides what AI is allowed to touch and who owns the call, every tool they buy helps individuals but never shows up on the P&L.

Meridian had three Yellows on the board. Which one to attack first wasn't obvious from the colors alone. Here's the rubric we used with them, and the one we use with every team that finds itself in the same spot.

1. **Foundation first.** Some Yellows unblock the others. Constraint Clarity is almost always the foundation: until the leadership team agrees on the one bottleneck, every other dimension is being scored against a moving target. If a Yellow row is a precondition for the others, it goes first.
2. **Highest pain inside reach.** Of the remaining Yellows, pick the one closest to the operational pain that brought you to the conversation. Not the most interesting Yellow, not the easiest Yellow, the one that sits on the workflow that's actually hurting.
3. **Smallest gap to Green.** When two Yellows are roughly tied on pain, pick the one with the smallest distance to Green. Yellow means you've got partial answer, document, or person. Less distance means a faster Green, and a fast Green builds credibility for the harder work behind it.
4. **Owner in the room.** Don't pick a Yellow that nobody on the leadership team owns. If you can't name the person who'll move it, you've picked a wish, not a constraint.
5. **Two-quarter horizon.** Pick the Yellow you can plausibly turn Green inside two quarters with the team you've got. If it's longer than that, the work is too big to be a single Sprint and needs to be broken down into a tighter constraint before Signal starts.

Apply the rubric in order. The first Yellow that passes all five is where you start. For Meridian, that meant Constraint Clarity first (foundation), then Workflow Visibility (highest pain inside reach, smallest gap to Green, Elena owns it). Measurement Discipline waited. Chapter 4 turns the chosen Yellow into a written constraint statement the leadership team can hold each other to.

Meridian's starting point: lock the quoting bottleneck as the constraint (turn Constraint Clarity from Yellow to Green), then map the end-to-end quoting workflow around it (turn Workflow Visibility from Yellow to Green). Those two moves created the foundation for everything that followed.

::: callout-tip
## Pro Tip

The AI Readiness Scorecard isn't a test. It's a map of where to start. If you're all Red, that's not a failure; it's the most honest answer most companies give. If you've got a Yellow, run it through the five-criterion rubric above and start there. You've already got something to build on.
:::

## Your map: the *Sprint Planning Canvas*.

The scorecard tells you where you're starting. The next thing you need is a map of where you're going. That map is the Sprint Planning Canvas.

If you run EOS, the Sprint Planning Canvas is the VTO equivalent. It is the single one-page document your leadership team fills in together as you work through the chapters ahead. The VTO is the one artifact that holds everything else in EOS together; the Sprint Planning Canvas plays the same role for Compound.

The Canvas has five sections.

1. **Constraint.** The one operational bottleneck you've decided to solve this Sprint, stated in one sentence with a dollar figure attached.
2. **Sequence first-pass.** One honest first guess per stage of the six-stage Sequence (Signal → Source → Design → Build → Deliver → Compound). The Sequence is defined in Chapter 3.
3. **Team.** Three to five people closest to the constraint workflow, plus a named Human Orchestrator who runs the Sprint day-to-day.
4. **Human Orchestrator.** The role that owns execution: cadence, handoffs, and the decision-making boundary between you and the AI workforce.
5. **Quarterly review.** The date you'll review the Sprint outcome with your leadership team. The Sprint is real when the review is on the calendar.

{{< excalidraw ch01-sprint-planning-canvas-empty "The Sprint Planning Canvas, empty: a one-page document with five sections (Constraint, Sequence first-pass, Team, Human Orchestrator, Quarterly review) populated across the remaining chapters." >}}

Every chapter from here forward fills in one section of this Canvas. Chapter 2 sets up the structural frame the Canvas sits inside. Chapter 3 defines the Canvas formally and shows a populated example. Chapters 4 through 9 walk the six stages of the Sequence, each one sharpening the row that stage owns. Chapter 10 sets the Quarterly review cadence. Chapter 11 hands you the worksheet for your first Sprint.

By the last page of this book, your leadership team has a filled-in Sprint Planning Canvas for your first Sprint, the next constraint already named, and the quarterly review on the calendar. That is the deliverable. Everything else is the work of producing it.

## What this *book* is for.

There is a name for the company that runs on the second question, the goal-oriented one from earlier in the chapter: *what outcomes are we accountable for, and how should the human + AI workforce be designed to deliver them?* We call that company the Co-Intelligent Company: a company where humans and AI operate as one system, where the work has been designed before the tool was deployed. That's where the Headcount Math moves.

This book gives you the Co-Operating Model to build that company: a specific sequence of stages with defined outputs at each step and a Sprint model you can run inside your existing meeting rhythms. The chapters ahead will show you what we did and give you the tools to replicate it.

The next chapter defines the Co-Intelligent Company precisely enough that you can locate yourself on the map and know where you're starting from. After that, you build.

::: callout-note
## Action Step

The scorecard is the input every other chapter references. Take an hour with your leadership team, ideally before your next L10, to score each dimension and write the scores down. Every chapter ahead will ask you to come back to them.
:::

## Reflection Questions

1.  Which of the five AI Readiness Scorecard dimensions scored lowest for your company — and does your leadership team agree on that score, or would each person give a different number?
2.  The chapter describes Meridian Manufacturing: two Reds and three Yellows. Walk into your next leadership meeting and ask the same question we asked Mark and Elena: what is the one operational problem this company keeps circling and never closes? Write down the answers verbatim, one per person. How much do they overlap, and what does that overlap (or its absence) tell you about whether you've got a constraint problem or an agreement problem?
3.  Are you running the wrong question? When your team discusses AI, does the conversation start with "what tasks could AI help with?" or "what outcomes are we accountable for, and how should human + AI deliver them?" Which framing dominated your last AI conversation?
4.  The Headcount Paradox says revenue and headcount move on a slope, and AI was supposed to bend it. Pull your own numbers: what is your revenue per employee today versus two years ago? Has the AI line item moved that number at all?
5.  Describe your operating model in three sentences: how work actually moves through your company, not the org chart. If you can't do it in three sentences, what does that tell you about where AI would even plug in?
